passage: The email to Professor Rao was four lines long. Damini had drafted it on Monday in her Hyderabad flat: could he please write a recommendation for her master's application? By Thursday it still sat in her drafts. Each evening she opened it, changed "Dear Sir" to "Respected Sir" and back again, then shut the laptop to wash dishes that were already clean. What if he didn't remember her? What if he said she wasn't strong enough? Lalremsiami, her flatmate, watched her scrub the same steel plate twice. "Is it the email again?" Damini nodded. "It'll take thirty seconds to send," Lalremsiami said. "I know," Damini said, and her voice cracked a little. "That's what makes it so stupid."

qa.q: How long was the email to Professor Rao?
qa.a: Four lines long.

qa.q: What was Damini worried about each time she opened the draft?
qa.a: That Professor Rao wouldn't remember her or would say she wasn't strong enough; the fear of that reply made a thirty-second task feel huge.

qa.q: What small step could help Damini send it tonight?
qa.a: Settling on one greeting and pressing send straight away, perhaps with Lalremsiami sitting beside her, so the dread gets no more evenings to grow.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami see Damini's week?
qa.a: Lalremsiami notices odd signs, like the same clean plate scrubbed twice, and gently names the email, seeing a small job weighed down by a big feeling.

grounding: An adult postpones a short recommendation request for days because she dreads the professor's reply.

passage:
"Tushar, you've been staring at that phone since dinner."
"It's nothing, Aai."
Ganga sat beside him on the diwan. "Nothing doesn't make you skip rice."
He sighed. "I made an error in the client sheet last week. I need to email my team lead and tell her."
"When did you find it?"
"Saturday."
"It's Wednesday, beta."
"I know!" He rubbed his eyes. "Every time I type it, I imagine her reply. Or no reply. Or a meeting invite with no title."
"How long is the email?"
"Three lines."
Ganga held out her hand. "Read it to me."
He read it. His voice shook on "my mistake".
"That's a good email," she said. "Clear. Honest."
"She'll be angry."
"Maybe. And then it'll be over. Right now it's been going on since Saturday."

qa.q: When did Tushar find the error?
qa.a: On Saturday.

qa.q: What does Tushar's shaking voice on "my mistake" suggest?
qa.a: He is frightened of how his team lead will react; saying the admission aloud makes that fear feel real, even in a three-line email.

qa.q: What choice does Ganga help Tushar make, and why does it help?
qa.a: She has him read the email aloud and tells him it is clear and honest, turning a dreaded message into a finished one he can send.

qa.q: How does Ganga see her son's evening?
qa.a: She notices he skipped rice and has been staring at his phone, and sees that waiting since Saturday is hurting him more than any reply might.

grounding: A young adult delays a three-line email admitting an error because he dreads his team lead's response.

passage: The email to Leela sat in my drafts for eleven days. I'd missed her wedding in March for a work trip I could have moved, and I knew it. The apology was five sentences; I wrote it on day one. Then every morning I'd open the laptop, see "Draft (1)", and suddenly remember fourteen other emails that needed replies first. I told myself I was waiting for the right words. Really I was waiting for a world where she wouldn't be hurt. On day eleven, a colleague asked why I kept sighing at my screen. I told him. He said, "Chetan, send it and go get tea." I did. Leela replied within an hour: "I was sad. Thank you for writing. Call me?"

qa.q: How long did the apology email sit in the drafts?
qa.a: Eleven days.

qa.q: What did Chetan want to avoid by waiting?
qa.a: A world where Leela wouldn't be hurt; sending the apology meant facing her reaction, and that dread made fourteen other emails suddenly feel urgent.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what could Chetan try next time?
qa.a: A colleague's nudge to send it and go get tea; next time Chetan could send a hard email right after writing it, before the dread has time to grow.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt during the eleven days of silence?
qa.a: Leela was already sad about the missed wedding, and each quiet day probably deepened it, which is why the apology, when it came, was welcome.

grounding: An adult keeps a five-sentence apology in drafts for eleven days because of dread about the friend's response.

passage: Selin had not opened the grant report in nine days. Every morning in her Copenhagen flat she told herself she was lazy and useless, and every morning the file felt heavier. On Tuesday she said it out loud while making coffee. "You're such a failure." Lars, her flatmate, looked up from his cereal. "Would you say that to me if I were late with something?" She blinked. "No. I'd say it happens." "So say that to yourself." It felt silly. She said, "Okay. I'm behind. It happens. Five minutes." She set the kitchen timer and opened the report. When it rang, she had fixed the title and one table. She reset it. Then again. By lunch the introduction was done, and the file felt lighter.

qa.q: What did Selin set before opening the report?
qa.a: The kitchen timer, for five minutes.

qa.q: Why did the file feel heavier each morning Selin called herself lazy?
qa.a: Each insult added guilt, so the report became a reminder of failure, and avoiding it felt like avoiding that bad feeling.

qa.q: What choice turned Tuesday around?
qa.a: Talking to herself the way she would talk to Lars, admitting she was behind without insults, and committing to only five minutes.

qa.q: What might Lars notice as Selin keeps resetting the timer?
qa.a: Lars sees his simple question working: the flatmate who was calling herself a failure over coffee is now calmly moving through the report.

grounding: An adult swaps self-criticism for a kind word and a five-minute start, and keeps going on a delayed report.

passage: At the insurance office in Kochi, Ayesha's compliance training was three weeks overdue. The reminder emails had turned from blue to red. At her desk she whispered, "Idiot. You had all of June." Then she opened the module and closed it again. Keerthana, who sat opposite and had been at the firm for years, rolled her chair over at teatime. "You look like you're fighting yourself." Ayesha admitted everything, the delay and the shame. Keerthana shrugged. "Half the floor is late on this one. Scolding yourself won't get you past slide one. Do five minutes before your tea goes cold. That's the whole job." Ayesha opened the module and clicked through the first slides. When the tea had gone cold she was on section two. She kept going till lunch.

qa.q: How overdue was Ayesha's compliance training?
qa.a: Three weeks overdue.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when she whispered "Idiot" at her desk?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and angry with herself for the delay, and that harshness made opening the module feel even worse, so she closed it again.

qa.q: What choice by Keerthana helped Ayesha start?
qa.a: Keerthana named the delay as common and set a tiny goal, five minutes before the tea went cold, which replaced shame with a doable step.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see Ayesha's struggle?
qa.a: With years at the firm, Keerthana recognises a familiar fight and treats it lightly, knowing kindness and a small start work better than scolding.

grounding: An adult stuck on overdue training is helped to drop self-blame and try five minutes, and then continues.

passage:
Sumit,
You asked how the thesis is going. Truth: I didn't touch it for all of September. Every night I'd lie awake calling myself a fraud and a waste of the scholarship, and the next morning I'd avoid it even harder. Then I remembered what you said when you failed your driving test: "I'm annoyed, not worthless." So last Monday I tried it. I wrote on a sticky note: "Behind, not broken. Five minutes." Just five. I opened chapter three, fixed two citations, and the timer went off. I didn't stop. It's been six days now, a little each morning. Some days it's only the five minutes, and I let that count. Thank you for that line. I didn't know I'd borrowed it until I needed it.
Mridul

qa.q: What did Mridul write on the sticky note?
qa.a: "Behind, not broken. Five minutes."

qa.q: Why did the nightly name-calling make the thesis harder to face?
qa.a: The harsh words filled Mridul with guilt, so each morning the thesis meant more shame, and avoiding it felt like the only relief.

qa.q: Which choice helped Mridul return to the thesis?
qa.a: Borrowing Sumit's kinder line and committing to five minutes, and letting even a five-minute day count, so starting stopped feeling like a verdict.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel reading that the line was borrowed?
qa.a: Sumit may be touched that a remark made after a failed driving test helped a friend out of a hard month, and glad to hear the thesis is moving.

grounding: An adult replaces nightly self-blame with a kind phrase and a five-minute start, and returns to the thesis.

passage:
Monday, first night of the new plan: Aparna's mother put up a paper chart: brush, pyjamas, one story, lights out at nine. Aparna argued at every step and brushed twice as slowly as usual.
Thursday, two weeks later: At ten to nine Aparna put down her crayons without being asked, went to brush, and came back holding the storybook.
Saturday, a month later, at Nani's house: There was no chart on the wall. But at nine Aparna yawned, found her toothbrush in the bag and climbed into bed with her book. Her little brother Akash was still bouncing on the mattress. "It's story time," Aparna told him, as if it were obvious.

qa.q: What four steps were on the paper chart?
qa.a: Brush, pyjamas, one story, lights out at nine.

qa.q: How can you tell the routine felt natural to Aparna by the Saturday at Nani's?
qa.a: With no chart, she yawned at nine and went to brush on her own, then told Akash "It's story time" as if it were obvious.

qa.q: What choice by Aparna's mother helped the steps become automatic?
qa.a: Keeping the same order at the same time every night, so nine o'clock began the whole chain without reminders.

qa.q: How might Akash see his sister's bedtime routine?
qa.a: Akash, still bouncing, may find it strange that she stops playing on her own, but her calm lead might pull him towards the story too.

grounding: A child's bedtime steps, repeated in the same order, become automatic even in a different house.

passage: Nilesh, you ask why I still fall asleep at nine sharp? Listen. When I was eight, in our village near Ludhiana, my Bebe had a fixed way. "Sleep comes on its own, Gurleen," she used to say. After dinner we rinsed our mouths at the hand pump and rubbed our teeth with a neem twig. Then we lay on the charpais in the courtyard, and she told one story, only one, about a clever crow or a lost princess. Then the lantern went out. Every night, the same order. After a few months, Nilesh, I would start yawning the moment I tasted the neem. My feet walked to the charpai by themselves. Seventy years later, I brush, I read one page, and I'm asleep. The body remembers what you repeat.

qa.q: What did the children rub their teeth with?
qa.a: A neem twig.

qa.q: Why did young Gurleen start yawning at the taste of neem?
qa.a: After months of the same order every night, the neem had become a signal that sleep came next, so the body got ready on its own.

qa.q: Which choice by Bebe made bedtime work so well?
qa.a: Keeping the same steps in the same order every night, rinse, one story, lantern out, so no step needed deciding.

qa.q: What might Nilesh take from this story?
qa.a: Nilesh may see that a steady bedtime order could make falling asleep easier, and it explains why the elder still sleeps at nine sharp.

grounding: An elder recalls how a fixed childhood bedtime order made sleep follow automatically.

passage: The wedding house in Madurai was loud until midnight, with music on the terrace and aunties laughing in every room. Kavitha, ten, was sure she would never sleep. But at half past eight she found her toothbrush in the suitcase, as she did every night at home. She brushed at the crowded sink, then went looking for her cousin Ayesha, who had promised to read to her. They squeezed onto a mattress in the storeroom, the only quiet corner, and Ayesha read one chapter by torchlight. Kavitha's eyes closed before the chapter ended. In the morning Ayesha said, "The music was so loud. How did you even sleep?" Kavitha shrugged. "It was bedtime."

qa.q: Where did Kavitha and Ayesha find a quiet corner?
qa.a: On a mattress in the storeroom.

qa.q: Why was Kavitha sure she would never sleep, and what changed?
qa.a: The house was loud with music and laughter, so sleep seemed impossible; but doing her usual steps made her body treat it as bedtime anyway.

qa.q: What choice helped Kavitha sleep despite the noise?
qa.a: Keeping her home routine, brushing at half past eight and hearing one chapter, even in a strange, crowded house.

qa.q: Why might Ayesha be surprised in the morning?
qa.a: Ayesha heard the music all night and expected a sleepless cousin, without realising how strongly the familiar steps carried Kavitha to sleep.

grounding: A child's usual bedtime steps carry her to sleep even in a noisy wedding house.

subtype: Reaching for the phone when bored [Actor]
passage: Between the physics and chemistry classes at the coaching centre there was a seven-minute gap. Nazia's hand was on her phone before the teacher had finished saying "break". She didn't open anything in particular: a cat video, a meme, somebody's new haircut, next, next. When Bidisha asked what she'd been watching, Nazia honestly couldn't say. It happened again in the lunch queue, waiting for the lift, and during the few seconds while the projector warmed up. On Friday the teacher collected every phone in a basket before a test. In the first empty minute Nazia's hand went to her pocket, found nothing, and she laughed out loud. "My hand went looking on its own," she whispered to Bidisha.

qa.q: How long was the gap between the physics and chemistry classes?
qa.a: Seven minutes.

qa.q: Why did Nazia laugh when her hand found an empty pocket?
qa.a: She was surprised to see her habit so clearly; she had not decided to reach for the phone, and catching her hand doing it alone felt funny and a little unsettling.

qa.q: What could Nazia try the next time a pause comes?
qa.a: Treat the empty moment as the cue and keep a different small action ready, like stretching or talking to Bidisha, with the phone zipped in her bag between classes.

qa.q: How does Bidisha experience Nazia's scrolling?
qa.a: Bidisha asks what Nazia watched and gets no answer, so Bidisha sees a friend who is busy but not really present in the gaps they share.

grounding: A teenager reaches for her phone in every pause without deciding to, showing a boredom-scroll-novelty loop.

subtype: Reaching for the phone when bored [Actor]
passage:
Dear Ritu didi,
You asked if I'm studying for boards. I'm trying, but I noticed something weird this week. Every time I finish a sum and there's a tiny pause while I think about the next one, my phone is already in my hand. I don't decide it. I just find myself scrolling: dance clips, recipe clips, somebody's cat. It's never anything I actually wanted. Yesterday I counted, and I picked it up thirty times in one hour of maths. Thirty! Each time there's a little buzz of "ooh, what's new", then I'm bored again and it's back in my hand. Amma thinks I'm lazy. I don't think it's that. I think my boredom and my hand have made some deal without me. How do you study?
Kalyani

qa.q: How many times did Kalyani pick up the phone in one hour of maths?
qa.a: Thirty times.

qa.q: What does Kalyani mean by saying boredom and the hand "made some deal"?
qa.a: Kalyani feels the scrolling runs by itself: a dull pause sets it off and a little buzz of something new pays it back, without any real decision.

qa.q: What small step could break the loop during maths?
qa.a: Keeping the phone in another room during sums and using each pause for a sip of water or a stretch, so the cue no longer leads straight to the screen.

qa.q: How might Ritu didi respond differently from Amma?
qa.a: Ritu didi may recognise the pattern from her own studying and treat it as a habit to redesign rather than laziness, and share what helps her.

grounding: A teenager notices that small pauses in study trigger automatic scrolling for a quick hit of novelty.

subtype: Reaching for the phone when bored [Actor]
passage: So, Thomas, remember when you said, "Noor, you're always on your phone"? You were right, and I didn't even know. Last week I tried an experiment for my psychology project. Every time I picked the phone up, I drew a tally on my wrist with a pen. By lunch my wrist was blue. And here's the weird bit: nearly every tally happened in a gap. Waiting for the bus. Teacher writing on the board. Microwave running. My brain hates empty seconds, apparently. I'd pick it up, see one new thing, get this tiny zing, and want the next one. Nothing I looked at was even good! On Thursday I left the phone in my locker and just stood at the bus stop being bored. It was horrible for about two minutes. Then I noticed the jacaranda tree.

qa.q: Where did Noor draw a tally each time the phone came out?
qa.a: On the wrist, with a pen.

qa.q: What was the "tiny zing", and why did it keep Noor reaching?
qa.a: It was the small thrill of seeing something new; that quick reward, not the content, made Noor want the next one, even when nothing was good.

qa.q: Which choice on Thursday showed a way out of the loop?
qa.a: Leaving the phone in the locker and staying with the boredom at the bus stop; after a couple of uncomfortable minutes, Noor noticed the jacaranda tree.

qa.q: How might Thomas feel hearing that the comment was right?
qa.a: Thomas may feel relieved that the comment landed as help rather than an attack, and curious to try the wrist-tally experiment.

grounding: A teenager tracks phone pick-ups and finds they come in empty moments, driven by a small reward of novelty.

passage: As her mother, I nagged Trisha about her phone for months. "Enough now," I'd call from the kitchen, and she'd say "five minutes", and those five minutes lasted till dinner. Then one afternoon I just watched instead of talking. She came home, dropped her bag, sat on the sofa, and the phone was in her hand before her shoes were off. The sofa was the start of it, every time. So I didn't lecture. I asked her to help me move the charging point from the sofa table to the shelf in my room, and we put a bowl of fruit and her sketchbook on the sofa instead. The first week she grumbled. By the third, she was sketching while she ate. I'm Deepika, by the way. I still nag, but much less.

qa.q: Where did Deepika and Trisha move the charging point?
qa.a: From the sofa table to the shelf in Deepika's room.

qa.q: Why might Trisha have said "five minutes" and then kept scrolling till dinner?
qa.a: She probably meant it, but the sofa set off the habit so strongly that the phone kept her before she noticed time passing.

qa.q: What choice did Deepika make instead of nagging, and why did it work?
qa.a: She changed the setting, moving the charger away and putting fruit and the sketchbook on the sofa, so the old cue led to something new.

qa.q: What was the change like for Trisha?
qa.a: At first Trisha grumbled at losing the easy phone spot, but by the third week she was sketching while she ate, without being told off.

grounding: A mother notices that her daughter's phone habit starts on the sofa and changes the setting rather than nagging.

passage:
Note for Nandini's school counsellor, from her mother, Farida
You asked me to notice when the phone habit starts, so I watched for a week without saying anything. It is almost always the same: Nandini comes in from school, sits in the big armchair by the window, and within a minute the phone is out. On the days she sits at the dining table instead, she eats and talks to me first. On Wednesday I moved the armchair to the balcony door and put the charger in the hallway. I didn't make a speech about it. She noticed, frowned, and sat at the table. We talked about her science teacher for twenty minutes. I will keep this setup for another week and tell you how it goes. I think the chair was doing more than I realised.

qa.q: Where did Farida move the armchair on Wednesday?
qa.a: To the balcony door, and the charger went into the hallway.

qa.q: What does Nandini's frown suggest she felt about the change?
qa.a: She was probably a little annoyed or thrown off to find her usual spot gone, yet the frown passed and she chose to sit at the table.

qa.q: Which choice by Farida worked better than nagging, and why?
qa.a: Watching quietly for a week, then moving the armchair and charger without a speech; changing the place removed the cue without starting a fight.

qa.q: How might the school counsellor read Farida's note?
qa.a: The counsellor would see a parent who looked for the pattern first and tested a small change, which gives useful evidence for helping Nandini further.

grounding: A mother watches her daughter's after-school phone habit, spots the armchair as its cue, and changes the setting instead of nagging.

passage:
14 Nov, night
Something clicked today. For weeks I've been snapping at Nirmala, "Phone down!", and she rolls her eyes and nothing changes. Today I came home early and saw exactly how it starts. She walked in, flopped on the diwan by the TV, and reached for the phone lying on the cushion, like her hand knew the way. She wasn't choosing anything. The diwan was choosing. So this evening I asked if she'd help me turn the diwan into a reading corner: a lamp, her comics, and the phone basket moved to the dining shelf. She thought I'd lost my mind. But she helped, and tonight she read two chapters there before she even remembered the phone. We'll see tomorrow. No more snapping from me.
Gurpreet (Papa)

qa.q: What did Gurpreet and Nirmala put in the new reading corner?
qa.a: A lamp and her comics, with the phone basket moved to the dining shelf.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet decide "the diwan was choosing"?
qa.a: Seeing Nirmala reach for the phone the moment she flopped down, he realised the spot itself set off the habit, so his snapping had been aimed at the wrong thing.

qa.q: What choice did Gurpreet make instead of snapping?
qa.a: He asked Nirmala to help rebuild the diwan as a reading corner and moved the phone basket away, changing the setting together with her.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see her father's sudden change?
qa.a: She first thinks he has lost his mind, but being asked to help rather than scolded probably felt better, and she read two chapters there.

grounding: A father sees that his daughter's phone habit begins on the diwan and changes the setting with her instead of nagging.

passage: Francis, you asked on your channel what my weirdest discovery of the semester was. Honestly? Biscuits. Every time an assignment email came in, my chest would tighten, and the next thing I knew I was at the hostel shop buying a packet. I'd eat half, feel calm for about ten minutes, then check the email again and go back for chips. I thought I just liked snacks. Then my roommate asked why I always ate right after reading my inbox, and it hit me. It wasn't hunger. The email was the trigger, the tight chest was the craving for calm, the biscuit was the relief. Once I saw the three pieces, I could choose where to cut in. Now when my chest tightens, I walk up to the terrace first. Samir's big discovery, folks.

qa.q: Where did Samir buy the biscuits?
qa.a: At the hostel shop.

qa.q: Why did buying a packet feel reasonable to Samir each time?
qa.a: The email made Samir's chest tighten, and the biscuits brought calm for about ten minutes, so from the inside it felt like fixing the stress, not a habit.

qa.q: What choice did Samir make once the three pieces were clear?
qa.a: To cut in at the craving: when the chest tightens, walk up to the terrace first, so the stress still gets relief without the snack run.

qa.q: How did the roommate's question change things?
qa.a: The roommate saw a pattern Samir couldn't, eating straight after the inbox, and one plain question let Samir see the loop's parts.

grounding: A stressed student sees that emails trigger a craving for calm that snacks briefly relieve, and changes the response.

passage: I'm Parveen, and I sit next to Imran in the architecture studio. I started noticing a pattern around jury week. Whenever Professor Mehta walked past and frowned at his model, Imran would pull out his phone and scroll. Not text anyone, just scroll, fast, for five or ten minutes. His shoulders would drop a bit. Then he'd look up, see the model, and his jaw would tighten again, and out came the phone. I don't know exactly what was happening in his head. But one evening, when the studio was quiet, he said, "Every time she frowns, I go numb on this thing and feel better for a bit." He'd noticed it too. The next day there was a sticky note on his desk: "Frown = go ask what's wrong."

qa.q: What did Imran write on the sticky note?
qa.a: "Frown = go ask what's wrong."

qa.q: What does the drop in Imran's shoulders suggest?
qa.a: Scrolling brought him brief relief from the stress of Professor Mehta's frown, which is why he kept going back to it.

qa.q: Which choice on the sticky note targets the loop, and why might it help?
qa.a: Replacing the scroll with asking what's wrong after a frown; it answers the real worry about the model instead of numbing it.

qa.q: How does Parveen see Imran's habit, and what can't Parveen know?
qa.a: Parveen sees the repeating frown-scroll-tighten cycle clearly, but admits to not knowing what is going on in his head until he says it himself.

grounding: A classmate observes a student whose stress at a frown triggers scrolling that gives brief relief, until he names the loop.

passage:
Sunday: Mohit had three chapters left before Tuesday's exam. Every time he opened the textbook his stomach knotted, and he reached for the chips on his desk and his phone. Twenty minutes of crunching and scrolling, and the knot eased. Then the textbook again, and the knot again. By midnight the packet was empty and he'd read four pages.
Monday: Sudha, his hostel neighbour, handed him a notebook. "Write down what happens right before you grab the chips." He did, all morning: "open chapter 5, stomach knots, grab." He stared at it. The knot was the starting point.
Tuesday, after the exam: "I kept a water bottle instead of chips and took three slow breaths whenever the knot came," he told Sudha. "Didn't fix everything. But I finished the chapter."

qa.q: What did Mohit write in the notebook on Monday morning?
qa.a: "Open chapter 5, stomach knots, grab."

qa.q: Why did the chips and scrolling feel helpful to Mohit on Sunday?
qa.a: They eased the knot in his stomach for a while, so they felt like the answer to the stress, even as the chapters stayed unread.

qa.q: What choice did Mohit make once he saw the knot was the starting point?
qa.a: He kept the cue but changed the response, a water bottle and three slow breaths instead of chips and the phone, and finished the chapter.

qa.q: What might Sudha feel hearing Mohit's report after the exam?
qa.a: Sudha may feel quietly pleased that the simple notebook idea helped Mohit see his loop, and glad he is honest that it didn't fix everything.

grounding: Across three days a student maps his stress-snack-scroll loop and changes the response at its starting point.

passage: Darshan wanted to run before college in the mornings, but in the first week he managed it only once. His shoes were in the tin trunk under the stairs, the socks somewhere else, and by the time he'd found both, the bus to Sinnar was due. So on Sunday he changed the setup. He put the shoes, socks tucked inside, right beside his charpai, and told himself the goal was only ten minutes: to the Hanuman temple at the end of the lane and back. "Ten minutes?" his friend Madhav scoffed. "That's not running." But on Monday Darshan's feet touched the shoes the moment he woke. He ran to the temple and back. Four weeks later he was still going, sometimes further, but never less than the temple.

qa.q: Where did Darshan put his shoes on Sunday?
qa.a: Right beside his charpai, with the socks tucked inside.

qa.q: Why was Darshan happy to set such a small goal despite Madhav's scoffing?
qa.a: Darshan wanted a start easy enough to happen every day; after a week of failed tries, ten minutes felt achievable rather than embarrassing.

qa.q: Which two choices helped the habit survive its first weeks?
qa.a: Keeping the shoes where his feet land on waking, and making the target tiny, to the temple and back, so there was nothing to hunt for and little to dread.

qa.q: How might Madhav's view change after four weeks?
qa.a: Madhav, who laughed at ten minutes, may be surprised that Darshan is still running and sometimes going further.

grounding: A student lowers friction by keeping shoes by the bed and setting a ten-minute target, and the running habit lasts.

passage: Anders had tried to start running three times since moving to Uppsala for university, and each time it died in the second week. Dark mornings, a cold floor, shoes lost somewhere in the hall cupboard. This time his flatmate Emil suggested something different. "Make it stupidly easy." So every night Anders laid out his running tights, jacket and shoes on the chair by his bed, and set the target at ten minutes on the lake path, nothing more. On the first morning he nearly skipped it, but everything was right there, so he pulled on the tights still half asleep. Ten minutes felt almost too short. He came back pink-cheeked and a little proud. Three weeks later the chair still held his kit every night, and Emil had started joining him.

qa.q: Where did Anders lay out his running kit each night?
qa.a: On the chair by his bed.

qa.q: How did Anders feel after the first ten-minute run, and why?
qa.a: He felt a little proud; after three failed starts, doing it at all, even briefly, showed him this attempt might be different.

qa.q: Which choice made the first morning work when Anders nearly skipped?
qa.a: Having everything laid out the night before, so he could pull on the tights half asleep without any search or decision.

qa.q: What would change for Anders if Emil stopped joining him later?
qa.a: The kit on the chair and the small target would still carry the habit, since the ease of starting, not company, is what got it going.

grounding: A student lays out running kit by the bed and sets a ten-minute goal, which helps the habit survive its early weeks.

passage: In the girls' hostel at Nandini's college, the sports track opened at six, but Nandini's alarm usually lost to her blanket. Her roommate Sunaina, who ran every day, suggested a trick. "Keep your shoes by your pillow. Literally. And promise yourself only ten minutes." So Nandini put her shoes at the head of the bed and her track pants on the chair. The first morning she grumbled but stepped straight into them. On the track she jogged slowly for ten minutes and walked back. "That's it?" Sunaina teased. "That's it," Nandini said. The next week she began adding a lap, but only when she felt like it. The deal stayed ten minutes. After a month, the track guard knew her name.

qa.q: What time did the sports track open?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: Why might Nandini have been happy to answer "That's it" to the teasing?
qa.a: She knew the small target was the point; keeping the promise to herself mattered more than impressing Sunaina, and it felt good to have gone at all.

qa.q: What choice kept the habit going once Nandini began adding laps?
qa.a: Keeping the deal at ten minutes and adding laps only when she felt like it, so a tired day never made starting feel too big.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see Nandini's progress over the month?
qa.a: Sunaina, a daily runner, may be pleased that the simple trick worked and enjoy seeing a roommate who used to lose to the blanket become a regular.

grounding: A student keeps shoes by the pillow and a ten-minute target, lowering friction so the running habit survives.

passage: Every time a client call went badly, Alka found herself on her phone for twenty minutes, thumb flicking, barely seeing anything. She had tried deleting the apps; she reinstalled them within the week. This time, at her office in Andheri, she tried something else. The cue would stay, that tight feeling after a hard call, but the answer would change. When a call ended, she would take the stairwell, down two floors and back up, breathing slowly. In a small notebook she ticked each time: walk or scroll, and how she felt afterwards. Jasleen, at the next desk, noticed the ticks. "What's that?" "Stairs versus scrolling," Alka said. By the end of the month the walk column was longer, and beside it she had written: "calmer, and I don't lose the afternoon."

qa.q: What did Alka tick in her small notebook?
qa.a: Walk or scroll, and how she felt afterwards.

qa.q: Why did deleting the apps not work for Alka?
qa.a: The stress after a hard call still needed an outlet, so without something else to meet that need she went back and reinstalled them.

qa.q: What choice made the change stick this time?
qa.a: Keeping the same cue but swapping the response for a stairwell walk with slow breathing, and tracking the result so she could see it worked.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see the "stairs versus scrolling" notebook?
qa.a: Jasleen may find it odd at first but interesting, seeing a colleague handle hard calls without disappearing into her phone.

grounding: An adult keeps the stress cue but replaces scrolling with a stairwell walk and tracks how it feels.

passage:
"Varun bhaiya, you've been on that phone since you walked in."
"Bad day. It helps."
Nitin sat on the arm of the sofa. "Does it?"
"For a bit." Varun kept scrolling. "Then I feel worse and keep going."
"You tried quitting last month."
"Lasted two days. When I'm stressed I need something."
"So have something. Just a different something." Nitin nodded at the balcony. "Remember how Papa used to go out and water the plants after a tense call with his boss? Ten slow breaths, then the tulsi."
Varun laughed. "That's so Papa."
"Try it for a week. Write down how you feel after each one, phone or balcony."
A week later a sheet hung on the fridge: five balcony ticks, two phone ticks, and "balcony = actually calmer" in Varun's messy handwriting.

qa.q: What was written on the sheet on the fridge a week later?
qa.a: Five balcony ticks, two phone ticks, and "balcony = actually calmer".

qa.q: Why did quitting the phone last only two days for Varun?
qa.a: When stressed he felt a real need for relief, and simply stopping left that need unmet, so the old habit came back.

qa.q: What choice did Nitin suggest, and why did it suit Varun?
qa.a: Swapping the phone for ten slow breaths and watering plants on the balcony, a familiar family habit that still gave him the break he needed.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel seeing the sheet on the fridge?
qa.a: Nitin may feel quietly proud that the suggestion helped, and relieved to see a calmer older brother after bad days.

grounding: A young adult replaces stress scrolling with breathing on the balcony, keeping the need for relief met, and tracks the result.

passage: Last spring my scrolling got bad. Every evening after my shift at the pharmacy I'd sit on the bed, tell myself "five minutes", and surface an hour later with stinging eyes, more wound up than before. I kept trying to just stop. It never lasted, because the need didn't go away: I was stressed and wanted a break. My friend Imran said, "Don't take the break away. Change what the break is." So I kept the same moment, sitting on the bed after work, and swapped the phone for five minutes of slow breathing by the open window. I made a chart and marked every evening: breathing or phone, and a number for how I felt. It took three weeks and some bad nights. But the breathing column won. I'm Usha, and I still sit on that bed every evening.

qa.q: What did Usha swap the phone for?
qa.a: Five minutes of slow breathing by the open window.

qa.q: Why did just stopping never last for Usha?
qa.a: The need behind the scrolling, stress and wanting a break, was still there, so without another way to meet it the phone kept winning.

qa.q: What choice made the change work, and what helped it last?
qa.a: Keeping the same moment on the bed but changing what the break was, and marking a chart each evening so the calmer nights became visible.

qa.q: How might Imran feel hearing that the breathing column won?
qa.a: Imran may feel glad the advice helped, and pleased that Usha stuck with it through three weeks and some bad nights.

grounding: An adult keeps the after-work cue but replaces stress scrolling with breathing, tracking results until it holds.

subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]
passage: "I'm bored," Santiago announced, ten minutes after lunch, flopping onto the rug of their flat in Lisbon. "Can I have the tablet?" His father, Kofi, shook his head. "Not now. You can have these." He put down three empty boxes, some string and a roll of tape. Santiago whined and kicked the rug. Kofi kept reading. After a while the whining stopped. Tape tore. When Kofi looked up, there was a box train across the floor, with a string whistle and a teddy driver. "Papa, you have to buy a ticket!"

qa.q: What did Kofi give Santiago instead of the tablet?
qa.a: Three empty boxes, some string and a roll of tape.

qa.q: How was Santiago feeling when he kicked the rug?
qa.a: He was cross and restless; being bored felt uncomfortable, and he wanted the tablet to make that feeling go away.

qa.q: Which choice by Kofi helped the boredom turn into play?
qa.a: Saying no to the tablet, handing over simple things and calmly waiting instead of rushing to fix the whining.

qa.q: What is it like for Kofi when Santiago asks him to buy a ticket?
qa.a: Kofi gets pulled into a game his son invented, probably enjoying seeing what came out of those bored minutes.

grounding: A young child declares boredom and wants a screen, but with time and simple materials he invents a game.

subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]
passage: During free time at the preschool, Dhruv sat on the floor and sighed loudly. "Manoj sir, I'm bored. Can I play on the computer?" "Not today," said Manoj sir, and put a basket beside him: leaves from the garden, some clay and two lids. "What can these become?" Dhruv pushed the basket away and lay on his back, staring at the fan. Manoj sir didn't hurry him. A few minutes later Dhruv sat up, pressed a leaf into the clay and looked at the print. Then another. By snack time he had a "leaf zoo" with a lid for a pond, and he was telling everyone who passed about each animal.

qa.q: What was in the basket Manoj sir put beside Dhruv?
qa.a: Leaves from the garden, some clay and two lids.

qa.q: What does Dhruv lying on his back and staring at the fan suggest?
qa.a: He was fed up and restless, not ready to play yet; the boredom felt unpleasant before an idea arrived.

qa.q: Which choice by Manoj sir let Dhruv's idea grow?
qa.a: Giving simple materials and then not hurrying him, so Dhruv had time to move from boredom to making something.

qa.q: How might the other children experience Dhruv's leaf zoo?
qa.a: They get a proud guide telling them about each animal, and may want to make prints of their own.

grounding: A preschool child says he is bored and asks for a screen, but with time and simple materials he creates a leaf zoo.

subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]
passage: I'm Harsha, Uday's big sister. On Sunday the power went off and the TV died, and Uday, who is five, lay on the floor moaning, "I'm SO bored. Give me your phone." I said no; the battery was low anyway. Amma just handed him an old bedsheet and some clothes pegs and went back to chopping onions. Uday cried a little. I thought he'd sulk all afternoon. But then it got quiet. When I peeked, he had pegged the sheet between two chairs and was sitting inside with a torch, whispering to his stuffed dog about "the cave rules". He didn't want to come out for dinner.

qa.q: What did Amma hand Uday?
qa.a: An old bedsheet and some clothes pegs.

qa.q: Why did Uday cry a little when he got the bedsheet instead of the phone?
qa.a: He wanted the boredom to end quickly with a screen, and being left with it felt unfair and uncomfortable at first.

qa.q: Which choice by Amma helped most, and why?
qa.a: Giving simple materials and going back to her work instead of entertaining him, which left space for Uday's own idea to appear.

qa.q: How does Harsha see what happened that afternoon?
qa.a: Harsha expected Uday to sulk all afternoon and is surprised to find him happily busy in a cave he built himself.

grounding: An older sister watches a bored five-year-old demand a phone, then build a pretend cave when given time and simple things.

subtype: Bored by a class that is too easy or too hard [Actor]
passage: The fans had stopped with the power cut, and forty-two students in Class 9B were sweating through a revision of fractions. Seema had done these in Class 6. By the third example she was drawing a detailed dragon in the margin. By the fifth, she was watching a crow on the window ledge. "Seema! Are you listening?" the teacher snapped. "Yes, miss." She wasn't. Jomon, beside her, was struggling with the same sums and copying every step. After class the teacher, still hot and tired, stopped at her desk and saw the dragon, then last week's test paper: full marks. "Is this too easy for you?" Seema hesitated. "A bit. I do them in my head." The teacher sighed and slid over a sheet of harder puzzles.

qa.q: What did Seema draw in the margin?
qa.a: A detailed dragon.

qa.q: Why did Seema drift off by the third example?
qa.a: She had done fractions years earlier, so the lesson gave her nothing to work on, and her attention went to the dragon and the crow.

qa.q: Which choice by the teacher helped, and what might have gone wrong without it?
qa.a: Checking her test paper and offering harder puzzles; without that, Seema could have been labelled lazy while her real need went unmet.

qa.q: How might Jomon experience the same lesson?
qa.a: For Jomon the lesson is hard enough to need every step, so the same class that bores Seema keeps Jomon busy and working.

grounding: A teenager doodles and stares out of the window because a hot, crowded revision class is far below her level.

subtype: Bored by a class that is too easy or too hard [Actor]
passage: In a third-floor classroom of his Kolkata school, Chetan's pen moved in slow circles, turning the corner of his notebook into a spiral galaxy. On the board, the chemistry teacher was balancing equations faster than he could follow. He had missed two weeks in July with typhoid and never caught up. Now each new line looked like code. He glanced at the window: pigeons, a tram bell, a man selling jhalmuri. Leela, who sat behind him, poked his back. "Aren't you going to copy this?" "What's the point?" he muttered. "I don't get the first step." At the break, Leela showed him her notes from July, and for the first time in weeks he asked a real question.

qa.q: Why did Chetan fall behind in chemistry?
qa.a: He missed two weeks in July with typhoid and never caught up.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he muttered "What's the point?"
qa.a: He felt lost and a little hopeless; without the first step the lesson made no sense, so copying felt useless.

qa.q: What turning point helped Chetan re-engage?
qa.a: Leela sharing the July notes at the break, which filled the gap so he could finally ask a real question.

qa.q: How might the chemistry teacher read Chetan's doodling if nobody explained?
qa.a: The teacher might see a pupil who doesn't care, when the doodling actually shows that the lesson is beyond him for now.

grounding: A teenager doodles and looks out of the window because a chemistry lesson is beyond him after missing weeks.

subtype: Bored by a class that is too easy or too hard [Actor]
passage:
"Your English teacher called," Amandeep said, putting down the phone. "She says you stare out of the window all period."
Chandrika shrugged. "It's boring."
"Boring? You love books."
"That's why! We're still on the same poem from July, Mummy. Line by line. I finished the whole textbook in the holidays."
"So you're not lazy, you're..."
"Waiting. For six weeks."
Amandeep sat down. "And maths? Your report says you're doodling there too."
Chandrika looked at her hands. "Maths is the opposite. I haven't understood anything since the new chapter. So I draw."
"Two different problems, then."
"Same face, though," Chandrika said, and almost smiled.
"Okay. I'll ask the school for harder reading for you, and we'll find someone to help with maths."

qa.q: How long has Chandrika's English class been on the same poem?
qa.a: Since July, for six weeks.

qa.q: What does Chandrika mean by "Same face, though"?
qa.a: She means she looks equally bored in both classes, even though one is too easy and the other too hard; she seems relieved her mother sees the difference.

qa.q: What choice does Amandeep make once she understands?
qa.a: Treating them as two different problems: asking for harder reading in English and finding help for maths, instead of scolding.

qa.q: How might the English teacher see Chandrika differently after hearing this?
qa.a: The teacher may stop reading the window-staring as disrespect and see a keen reader who needs more challenge.

grounding: A teenager looks bored in two classes for opposite reasons, one too easy and one too hard, and her mother sees the mismatch.
